newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudan former minister sees dim ceasefire chances.
newsitem.headline: Sudan former minister sees dim ceasefire chances.

text.p: Sudan's exiled opposition leader Sadeq al-Mahdi said he expected an African initiative to end 14 years of civil war in Sudan to yield limited results but ruled out a ceasefire agreement.
"I think there is great probability that the IGAD mediation will result in...getting talks started," Mahdi told the Foreign Press Association in Cairo on Thursday night.
He said a ceasefire was "now not in question", and that the Sudan government offer for one was motivated by an attempt to "gain time" because it felt "the military squeeze".

Mahdi, a former prime minister, was commenting on Sudan President Omar Hassan al-Bashir's call on Tuesday for a ceasefire in the war with Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) rebels, led by John Garang, in the south of the country.
Bashir's call during a visit to South Africa took place against the background of an African peace initiative under the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD).
Bashir's government and Garang's rebels are expected to hold talks in the IGAD initiative framework in Nairobi starting on August 19.
"I think the response of Garang to the initiative of IGAD...has been positive, and whatever process will be started will be under the umbrella of the IGAD," Mahdi said.

But he said the "IGAD formula" must be updated in terms of the parties and agenda. "Unless the parties to the conflict are more realistically appreciated, I think the whole exercise will not produce any results."
IGAD groups Kenya, Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Uganda, Somalia and Djibouti, and aims to help settle conflicts in the region.

Mahdi is a member of the Sudanese opposition National Democractic Alliance (NDA), an umbrella of northern and southern rebels, including the SPLA, fighting to topple the Sudanese Islamist government. Mahdi said he spoke to Garang this week.

"I think he has accepted the principles of talking...Garang is a leading member of the NDA, which has not been invited and the NDA has not decided on its response on this issue...since it was not invited" to the IGAD meeting, he said.
The war in Sudan pits Christian and animist rebels in the south against the Moslem and Arabised north. The rebels want greater autonomy or independence from the north.
Bashir's government toppled Mahdi in a coup in 1989. Mahdi is on the exiled opposition's leadership council.
The Sudan government signed an accord with six rebel groups in April, but the SPLA rejected it and refuses to agree to a ceasefire with Khartoum.

Mahdi said there were divisions in Sudan's ruling National Islamic Front (NIF) which he described as a "hydra-head" where an "internal cold war" was taking place. He said a "main schism" was between Bachir and parliament speaker Hassan al-Turabi.
"I think the only really acceptable compromise is for this regime to quit," said Mahdi. "The only possible compromise is that of peaceful liquidation of the regime."
